    Same-section registration¶

    When a second modality is imaged on the same physical section as your spatial transcriptomics run (for example, a nuclear stain done after Xenium), every nucleus sits in one Xenium cell. Registration is then a correspondence problem: find the transform that puts each nucleus back in its cell, then snap the confident pairs exactly onto their partners.

    In this tutorial you will:

    1. register a synthetic nuclei / cell pair with a known misalignment using register_centroids (method multiround), and check the result against the truth;
    2. snap matched nuclei onto their cells with refine_by_assignment, and read its statuses and neighbour_deviation;
    3. repeat both steps on a 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm crop of real data (Sample 2, section z5);
    4. do the same from CSV files in one call, as the command line does.

    Runtime: under a minute on a laptop CPU. Requires: SMINT only (no GPU, no Cellpose, no STalign).

    Data. The synthetic files are made by python examples/make_tutorial_data.py and, like the Sample 2 crop, ship with the repository in docs/tutorials/data/. Run this notebook from docs/tutorials/ so the relative data/ paths resolve.

    Download this notebook: 02_same_section_registration.ipynb

    import logging
import sys

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Show SMINT's progress messages in the notebook
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
                    stream=sys.stdout, force=True)
# The deprecated xenium_metabolomics module warns when STalign is absent; it is not used here
logging.getLogger("smint.alignment.xenium_metabolomics").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
# Per-call matching messages are very chatty; keep the round-by-round summary
logging.getLogger("smint.alignment.centroid_registration").addFilter(
    lambda record: not record.getMessage().startswith("Matched "))

from smint.alignment import alignment_quality, refine_by_assignment, register_centroids

CELL, NUC, ASSIGNED = "#2b6cb0", "#d53f8c", "#dd8a2e"


def status_legend(fig, pairs=True):
    """One legend for the three-panel figures: cells, and nuclei by status."""
    from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
    dot = lambda c, label: Line2D([], [], ls="", marker="o", ms=5, color=c, label=label)
    handles = [Line2D([], [], ls="", marker="o", ms=9, mfc="none", mec=CELL, label="Xenium cell"),
               dot(NUC, "nucleus (right panel: snapped)"), dot(ASSIGNED, "assigned"),
               dot("0.55", "filled (moved with neighbours)")]
    if pairs:
        handles.append(Line2D([], [], color="0.6", lw=0.8, label="line to true partner"))
    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower center", ncol=len(handles), frameon=False,
               bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02))

    1. Load the synthetic pair¶

    synthetic_cells.csv plays the Xenium cells (the target, fixed) and synthetic_nuclei.csv the post-stain nuclei (the source, moved). The nuclei were displaced by about 17 µm — roughly one cell spacing, which is what makes this hard — plus a 0.5° rotation, a 0.6% scale change and a smooth warp of a few microns. As in real data, about 10% of cells have no nucleus and there are extra nuclei with no cell.

before registration: {'median_nn': 12.86, 'mutual_within_5': 0.08, 'mutual_within_10': 0.29}

    alignment_quality is a correspondence-free summary: median_nn is the median distance from each nucleus to its nearest cell, and mutual_within_5 the fraction of nuclei whose nearest cell has them as its nearest nucleus too, within 5 µm. Before registration few nuclei are mutual neighbours of their cell.

    def panel(ax, cells, xy, title, window, colors=NUC, pairs=None):

    Most nuclei sit between two cells, and the nearest cell is often the wrong one. Matching every nucleus to its nearest cell and fitting a transform to those pairs — what the single-round methods do — would fit mostly wrong pairs.

    2. Register with multiround¶

    register_centroids with the default method="multiround" never commits to individual pairs early. It cuts the section into blocks, lets every nucleus vote for the displacements to several nearby cells, and takes the peak of the votes in each block — the true offset is the one the whole block agrees on. Round 1 fits an affine through the block peaks; round 2 votes again in smaller blocks and adds a smooth thin-plate spline. A round is kept only if it improves the alignment.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    result = register_centroids(nuclei_xy, cells_xy)   # method="multiround", max_distance=100

    The log is the per-round summary that is also stored in result["rounds"]:

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    pd.DataFrame(result["rounds"]).round(2)
    pd.DataFrame(result["rounds"]).round(2)
    Out[5]:
    stage median_nn max_distance block_size blocks consistent_blocks accepted
    0 initial 12.90 NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN
    1 affine 3.60 100.0 500.0 16.0 1.00 True
    2 tps 3.25 25.0 250.0 64.0 0.86 True

    How to read it:

    • blocks / consistent_blocks — how many blocks had enough nuclei to vote, and the fraction whose peak agrees with the fitted model (RANSAC inliers). A low fraction means the blocks disagree: check the data before trusting the round.
    • median_nn — the median nucleus-to-nearest-cell distance for the fitting nuclei after that round. It should fall.
    • accepted — whether the round improved median_nn by at least min_improvement (1%). The first rejected round ends the schedule.

    A quarter of the nuclei (validation_fraction=0.25) were held out before any voting. tre_validation is measured on them only — it is the number to trust.

    Because this is synthetic data you can also score the transform against the truth — the distance from each moved nucleus to where it really belongs:

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    smooth_xy = result["transform"](nuclei_xy)
has_cell = true_cell >= 0
before = np.linalg.norm(nuclei_xy - true_xy, axis=1)[has_cell]
after = np.linalg.norm(smooth_xy - true_xy, axis=1)[has_cell]
print(f"true error, median: {np.median(before):.1f} um before -> {np.median(after):.2f} um after")
print(f"true error, 95th percentile after: {np.percentile(after, 95):.2f} um")
    smooth_xy = result["transform"](nuclei_xy) has_cell = true_cell >= 0 before = np.linalg.norm(nuclei_xy - true_xy, axis=1)[has_cell] after = np.linalg.norm(smooth_xy - true_xy, axis=1)[has_cell] print(f"true error, median: {np.median(before):.1f} um before -> {np.median(after):.2f} um after") print(f"true error, 95th percentile after: {np.percentile(after, 95):.2f} um")
    true error, median: 18.0 um before -> 1.20 um after
true error, 95th percentile after: 2.89 um

    The transform recovers the misalignment to about a micron. The held-out TRE is larger than that because it measures distance to the nearest cell centroid, and nuclei sit a few microns off-centre in their cells.

    3. Snap nuclei onto their cells¶

    A smooth transform cannot put every nucleus exactly on its cell. refine_by_assignment does that in a second step:

    1. pair moved nuclei and cells as mutual nearest neighbours within snap_radius (10 µm);
    2. keep a pair only if its offset agrees with the median offset of the pairs around it (within consistency_tol, default 0.4 × the cell spacing) — a nucleus paired with the wrong cell disagrees with its neighbourhood;
    3. move kept nuclei exactly onto their cell (snapped); move the rest by the median offset of their snapped neighbours (filled) and try pairing again, up to passes times;
    4. pair leftover filled nuclei with still-free cells by a one-to-one minimum-distance assignment (assigned) — these skipped the neighbourhood check, so they are less certain.
    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    refined = refine_by_assignment(nuclei_xy, cells_xy, transform=result["transform"])
status = refined["status"]
print(pd.Series(status).value_counts().to_string())
print(f"snapped per pass: {refined['snapped_per_pass']}")
print(f"cells that received a nucleus: {refined['fraction_targets_matched']:.1%}")
    refined = refine_by_assignment(nuclei_xy, cells_xy, transform=result["transform"]) status = refined["status"] print(pd.Series(status).value_counts().to_string()) print(f"snapped per pass: {refined['snapped_per_pass']}") print(f"cells that received a nucleus: {refined['fraction_targets_matched']:.1%}")

    The synthetic truth says which cell each nucleus belongs to, so you can check every placement:

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    partner = refined["target_idx"]
rows = []
for s in ("snapped", "assigned", "filled"):
    k = status == s
    rows.append({
        "status": s, "nuclei": int(k.sum()),
        "on the right cell": f"{np.mean(partner[k] == true_cell[k]):.1%}" if s != "filled" else "-",
        "nuclei with no cell": f"{np.mean(true_cell[k] < 0):.1%}",
        "median neighbour_deviation (um)": round(float(np.nanmedian(refined['neighbour_deviation'][k])), 1)
                                          if s != "filled" else "-",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("status")
    partner = refined["target_idx"] rows = [] for s in ("snapped", "assigned", "filled"): k = status == s rows.append({ "status": s, "nuclei": int(k.sum()), "on the right cell": f"{np.mean(partner[k] == true_cell[k]):.1%}" if s != "filled" else "-", "nuclei with no cell": f"{np.mean(true_cell[k] < 0):.1%}", "median neighbour_deviation (um)": round(float(np.nanmedian(refined['neighbour_deviation'][k])), 1) if s != "filled" else "-", }) pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("status")
    Out[9]:
    nuclei on the right cell nuclei with no cell median neighbour_deviation (um)
    status
    snapped 3585 98.9% 1.1% 2.5
    assigned 64 45.3% 53.1% 8.1
    filled 952 - 97.4% -

    Snapped nuclei are almost all on the right cell. Assigned ones are much less reliable: many are nuclei that have no cell of their own, placed on a neighbour's. neighbour_deviation tells them apart without any truth — it is the distance between a pair's offset and its snapped neighbourhood's median offset: about the nucleus-in-cell scatter for a right pair, about a cell spacing for a wrong one. SMINT logs a warning when assigned pairs deviate much more than snapped ones, as above; filter on neighbour_deviation or pass assign_remaining=False if you need only confident pairs.

    4. Real data: Sample 2, section z5¶

    The same two calls on a 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm crop of real data: nuclei segmented from a stain done after the Xenium run, and the Xenium cells of that section. Coordinates are in microns, re-origined to the crop corner. There is no truth here, so the held-out numbers and the plots are the checks.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    cells = pd.read_csv("data/sample2_xenium_z5_crop.csv")
nuclei = pd.read_csv("data/sample2_nuclei_z5_crop.csv")
cells_xy = cells[["x_centroid", "y_centroid"]].to_numpy()
nuclei_xy = nuclei[["centroid_x", "centroid_y"]].to_numpy()
print(f"{len(cells_xy):,} Xenium cells, {len(nuclei_xy):,} nuclei")

result = register_centroids(nuclei_xy, cells_xy)
pd.DataFrame(result["rounds"]).round(2)

    5. From files, in one call¶

    register_centroid_files reads both CSVs, registers, refines and writes the whole source table back with new columns. The smint-alignment centroid command runs exactly this (see Command line).

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    from smint.alignment import register_centroid_files

table, result = register_centroid_files(
    "data/sample2_nuclei_z5_crop.csv",            # source: centroid_x / centroid_y
    "data/sample2_xenium_z5_crop.csv",            # target: x_centroid / y_centroid
    output_path="nuclei_registered.csv",
)
table.head()
    from smint.alignment import register_centroid_files table, result = register_centroid_files( "data/sample2_nuclei_z5_crop.csv", # source: centroid_x / centroid_y "data/sample2_xenium_z5_crop.csv", # target: x_centroid / y_centroid output_path="nuclei_registered.csv", ) table.head()

    Column Meaning
    x_transformed, y_transformed Final position: on the partner cell for snapped / assigned nuclei, otherwise the filled position
    x_transformed_smooth, y_transformed_smooth Position after the smooth transform only
    registration_status snapped, assigned, filled or unmoved
    target_index Row of the partner cell in the target file, -1 if none
    neighbour_deviation Disagreement with the snapped neighbourhood, in µm (NaN when not placed)

    The same run from a terminal:

    smint-alignment centroid \
    --source data/sample2_nuclei_z5_crop.csv \
    --target data/sample2_xenium_z5_crop.csv \
    --output-dir z5_crop_registration

    Add --submit --watch to run it as a SLURM job instead (see Running on HPC).
